summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors, and Aceh operates inside that national framework rather than alongside it. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Aceh is the only province in Indonesia operating a codified religious criminal law of its own, the Qanun on jinayat (No. 6/2014). Same-sex conduct falls under the headings liwath and musahaqah.

Public caning is the standing punishment for sharia offences in Aceh. On 26 August 2025 two men were publicly caned in the provincial capital after a sharia court convicted them of hugging and kissing. Two men were also publicly caned in the province in February 2025 for a same-sex relationship.

Physical risk extends beyond the courts. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge directly to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism, placing them inside national defence policy.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying gay or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Documents and status are restrictive. Indonesia recognises only male and female sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Transgender women face the highest rates of violence among LGBTIQ Indonesians, according to survey data reported by the UNSW Human Rights Research Centre, which also documents the January 2018 detention of twelve transwomen. That evidence is national in scope rather than specific to Aceh, but it describes the population most exposed to the enforcement pattern seen in the province.

Local scholarship at UIN Ar-Raniry reads the rising number of waria in Banda Aceh through a law-enforcement lens, treating waria visibility as a case problem for sharia administration rather than as a question of rights. The QURU: Journal of Family Law and Culture framing indicates that academic work in Aceh is organised around how religious law should reach gender-nonconforming residents.

Aceh's reliance on corporal punishment distinguishes it from the other criminalising province, South Sumatra, which applies national-level provisions without a qanun of its own. A visitor's exposure in Aceh therefore includes a sentence type that does not arise elsewhere in Indonesia.
localsOnly:
Residents of Aceh answer to the Qanun on jinayat (No. 6/2014) as well as national law, and public caning is the routine sentence for sharia offences, applied after conviction by a sharia court.

Waria in Banda Aceh face sustained law-enforcement attention; local legal scholarship treats their growing numbers as an enforcement challenge, which shapes how police and religious officers engage with gender-nonconforming residents in practice.

Indonesian residents have no statutory protection against discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and legal gender recognition is available only through sex reassignment surgery plus a court order.

Because no third-gender marker exists on Indonesian identity documents, waria and other gender-diverse residents present documents that do not match their lived gender in every routine interaction, from banking to policing.
outOfScopeNotes:
The specific penalties attached to liwath and musahaqah under the Qanun on jinayat, and the number of caning strokes authorised, are not stated in the available sources for this pass.

How often the qanun is enforced against trans residents of Aceh, as distinct from cisgender men, remains unresolved; the UIN Ar-Raniry article is cited here for its framing rather than for case counts, which have not been extracted.

Whether Aceh sharia courts have prosecuted trans people under the qanun, and with what outcomes, is not sourced in this inventory.

The January 2018 detention of twelve transwomen is documented in a report covering Indonesia as a whole; whether comparable detentions have occurred in Aceh specifically is not established.

No Aceh-specific data is available on facilities access, healthcare availability for trans travellers, or entry screening practices at the province's points of arrival.
